newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS confirms Nazi gold deals, opens archives.
newsitem.headline: BIS confirms Nazi gold deals, opens archives.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) on Monday released a detailed account of its Nazi gold transactions and pledged to open its secretive wartime archives to the public from July.
The BIS board of directors, made up of central bank governors from the Group of Ten (G10) industrialised countries, also decided to make available all documents older than 30 years from January 1998.
The report, which was audited by Coopers & Lybrand, confirmed earlier BIS statements that Hitler's Reichsbank transferred 13.5 tonnes of gold to BIS between 1939 and 1945.
A final shipment of 1.5 tonnes in April 1945 never reached Switzerland because it was stopped at the German-Swiss border.
After World War Two, BIS handed back 3.7 tonnes of the gold to the Allied powers after it was identified as looted by Germany from the central banks of Belgrium, Italy and the Netherlands.
BIS general manager Andrew Crockett told a news conference the report gives a detailed "bar by bar" account of its Nazi gold dealings.
Crocket said the report was a factual accounting and did not delve into the issue of whether dealing with Nazi Germany was morally justified.
"It is fair to say our original focus has been to establish facts rather than to try to guess the motivations and opinions (of wartime BIS management)," Crockett said.
"The facts are there and I prefer to let others judge whether the behaviour of BIS was appropriate during the war."
BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, has been preparing to open its archives for the last two years after keeping them hermetically sealed for decades.
It said the board had now decided to open the archives to researchers and historians from next January.
"However, as a preliminary measure, major documents relating to BIS's wartime activities will be made available to historians and researchers from July this year," a BIS statement said.
These documents will include all files used in drafting the Nazi gold report, it added.
BIS released the gold report to put an end to speculation over its wartime role, which was heavily criticised by the Allied powers during and after the war.
BIS was created in 1930 to oversee German reparations after World War One.

About half the gold sent to BIS by the Reichsbank was for German interest payments on reparations and the other half covered German debts in a European postal clearing system and payments to Yugoslav railways.
"Our responsibility in this generation is to make sure that everything that is available to be known is there so history can make its judgement," Crockett said.

The report is based on a detailed account the BIS sent last year to U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, who has spearheaded U.S. inquiries into the fate of gold stolen by the Nazis and sold to Switzerland's central bank as well as the whereabouts of dormant Jewish accounts in Swiss commercial banks.
BIS is an international organisation but has been drawn into the debate about the Swiss role because it also accepted gold from Nazi Germany.
